The old boat shed was a place of industry, the briny air thick with the smell of tar and hemp. A single great lantern, hung from a central rafter, did what it could to beat back the evening; it laid a trembling, golden path across the worn floorboards from the door to the water’s edge; it made the coils of new rope gleam like sleeping serpents; and it gave the high-heaped nets, mounded in the corner, the look of some strange, fibrous hillock from a dream. All else was shadow, a deep and shifting dark that hid the cobwebbed eaves and played tricks with the eye. The figures moving within this circle of light seemed less like men and more like allegories of labour, their faces and forms captured for a moment in Rembrandt-like richness before being swallowed again by the gloom.

There was old Martin, his face a roadmap of sea-weathered wrinkles, looking for all the world like some ancient mariner from a storybook, his gnarled hands working a wooden needle through the mesh with a practiced rhythm that was a wonder to behold. There was Mr. Ainsworth, the new curate, who had come down to the shore to offer, as he put it, "a hand of fellowship to the fishing folk," though his own hands were white and unaccustomed to the work, and his efforts to untangle a particularly stubborn knot had thrown his usually placid features into such a mask of comical frustration that he might have been a tragic actor rehearsing a difficult part. Young Will, whose job was to fetch and carry the heavy hanks of twine, was simply Will; the light could do nothing to dignify his lanky awkwardness or the perpetual smudge of dirt on his nose. But when his mother, Martha, came to the door with a steaming jug, her kind, broad face framed by the darkness, she appeared a very Madonna of the harbour.

Eleanor had been watching from the doorway for some minutes, content to be a spectator to the humble drama, before stepping forward with the quiet purpose of a lady inspecting her gardens, to approve and encourage the efforts of her tenants. The curate, seeing her, immediately abandoned his knot with a look of profound relief.

"Ah, Miss Croft! A welcome sight. Your man Martin here is a true artist with his needle."

"We'll have 'em mended afore the tide turns, miss," Martin said, not looking up from his work; "long as the weather holds. It's been a right good season for mackerel, the best I've seen in a decade. The nets took a tearin' yesterday though, on account of a snag we caught on the bottom. I reckon it was an old wreck; there's a dozen of 'em out past the point."

"Indeed," put in Mr. Ainsworth, brushing pieces of twine from his black coat. "A proper mending is paramount to future success. I was just suggesting to Martin that a double stitch along the primary stress points might add a degree of fortification to the apparatus. It is a principle I have observed in tailoring."

"A double stitch'll make her too stiff, sir," said Martin, with the patient air of one explaining the obvious. "A net's got to have give in it, see? It's got to stretch with the weight o' the fish and the pull o' the water. You make it too strong in one spot, and it'll just tear in another that ain't so strong; and you'll have a worse mess than you started with. A simple weaver's knot, pulled tight and true, that's all she needs."

"A fascinating counterpoint," said the curate, looking doubtfully at the net. "The paradox of strength through flexibility. One might draw a sermon from it."

"You might do," said Martin, biting off a thread with his teeth, "but you won't catch no mackerel with it."

Eleanor smiled at the exchange, when a voice spoke quietly beside her, making her start. It was Mr. Reed, the naturalist who was lodging in the village for the autumn.

"I called at the house," he said, "and your housekeeper sent me in this direction. I hope I am not intruding on a council of war."

"Only a very peaceful one, about the science of net-mending," Eleanor replied. "You see what great matters we concern ourselves with here. Are we not a picturesque study?"

He looked not at the scene, but at her. "Very," he said, then seemed to catch himself. "The light is quite remarkable. It turns the whole affair into a painting. Look at young Will now, with that coil of rope over his shoulder; he is like a figure preparing the ropes for some great expedition. It is quite striking, is it not, Miss Croft?"

"I think so," she said. "I have always found it so. You see things with an artist's eye, Mr. Reed, and find the beauty I only feel."

"That young lady, sir," declared Mr. Ainsworth from across the shed, gesturing with a length of twine, "that young lady possesses a most admirable sympathy with the working classes."

"A sympathy!" said Mr. Reed softly, for Eleanor's ear alone.

"He means I bring them cider on hot days," she murmured back.

"Miss Croft, Mr. Reed," the curate continued, his voice warming to his subject, "Miss Croft, sir, understands that the--a--the sinews of our great nation are its industrious poor, and she provides a model of benevolent proprietorship."

"I won't say she's not a good landlord," Martin grumbled, still focused on his work, "for she is; keeps the cottages in good repair, which is more than her father did!"

This frank assessment made Mr. Reed's lips twitch, and even Mr. Ainsworth was momentarily silenced.

"You see," Eleanor said, turning to walk with Mr. Reed toward the door and the fresh night air, "I am a celebrated patron of industry."

"So I gather," he answered, his smile now open. "And a repairer of cottages. But I suspect--forgive me--that you carry burdens much heavier than a jug of cider."

Her own smile faded a little, and she looked out toward the dark, murmuring sea.

"The sea carries many burdens," she answered, her voice so low that it was nearly lost in the steady sigh of the surf upon the shingle below. "It is a better keeper of secrets than I am."

"I beg your pardon," he said quickly, his tone one of genuine contrition. "It was an impertinent remark. The light and the hour, perhaps, lend themselves to unguarded thoughts. We should not have left the cheerful industry of the shed."

"No, no, do not say so," Eleanor replied, turning her face toward him, though it was little more than a pale oval in the darkness. "I am grateful for the quiet. The industry, as you call it, is cheerful for an hour's viewing; but it is their whole life, Mr. Reed, and the cheerfulness is sometimes a thin coat over a great deal of anxiety. Martin's good humour depends entirely upon the strength of his nets and the prospect of the herring."

"And your good humour?" he asked, so gently that the question seemed less an inquiry and more a simple reflection of her own words.

She did not answer immediately, but walked on a few paces. They had turned from the boat-shed and taken the narrow track that led along the top of the low cliffs; a path worn smooth by generations of fishermen and coastguards, with the dark expanse of the sea on their one hand, and the sleeping fields of the parish stretching away on the other. The moon had not yet risen, but the sky was full of a soft, starlight lustre that kept the darkness from being absolute.

"My good humour," she said at last, "is a more complicated piece of machinery. It depends upon Martin's good humour, and Mrs. Gable's rheumatics, and the price of corn in Norwich, and whether the thatch on the old barns will last another winter. It is a landlord's humour, I suppose; a poor sort of thing, made up of other people's prosperities and misfortunes."

"I think it a very noble sort of thing," he said. "To have one's own peace so bound up with the welfare of others."

"It is not noble, it is merely necessary," she returned, with a touch of impatience that was more with her situation than with him. "When the estate passed to me, it was not in the best of health. My father--my father had a more sanguine temperament than I, and believed that matters would always right themselves in the end. I have found they require a good deal of pushing and pulling before they will even consent to stand still."

"Like Martin's nets," Mr. Reed suggested. "A constant mending and tending, lest the whole enterprise give way."

She was struck by the comparison, and by the quickness with which he had understood her. "Precisely," she said, her voice softening again. "A constant mending. And sometimes one feels that one is using the wrong sort of thread, or that the holes are appearing faster than one can possibly patch them." She paused, and gave a little, self-deprecating laugh. "You see what a poor companion I am, Mr. Reed. You came for a picturesque study of village life, and I give you a lecture on estate management."

"I find this lecture infinitely more interesting," he declared. "The picturesque is for a sketchbook; but this is the living reality. I should count it a privilege if you would sometimes allow me to see the ledger-book, as you called it, instead of only the painting."

Before Eleanor could frame a reply to this rather earnest speech, a slightly breathless voice hailed them from behind. "Miss Croft! Mr. Reed! A moment, if you please!"

It was Mr. Ainsworth, the curate, hurrying to catch them up, his long coat flapping about his ankles. "I feared I had lost you in the gloom," he panted, coming alongside them. "An admirable night for a constitutional, is it not? Though the air has a certain--a--a certain dampness which one must be wary of."

"We were just remarking upon the beauty of the scene, Mr. Ainsworth," said Eleanor, her tone regaining its usual placid composure.

"Ah, yes! The sublime," the curate agreed, gesturing vaguely toward the dark water. "The vast, illimitable ocean. A powerful reminder of our own insignificance in the grand scheme of the Creator's works. And yet," he added, turning his attention back to them, "it is in our small, terrestrial duties that we find our truest purpose. As I was remarking to young Will just now, a well-mended net is a work of piety in its own way."

"I am sure Will was greatly edified," said Eleanor, with a smile that Mr. Reed, by her side, could just discern.

"Indeed, indeed. But I was seeking you out, Miss Croft, on a particular matter. I have been speaking with Mr. Giles, the churchwarden, about the Harvest Festival. He is of the opinion, and I am inclined to agree, that the east window requires a more--a--a more elaborate treatment this year. We thought perhaps a sheaf of corn, bound with red ribbon, on either side; and a display of marrows and other gourds upon the sill itself. I wished to solicit your opinion, as our chief patroness and a lady of acknowledged taste."

"That sounds very fine, Mr. Ainsworth," Eleanor said patiently. "I am certain whatever you and Mr. Giles decide will be most appropriate."

"Yes, but the question of procurement arises," the curate pressed on. "The finest sheaves, of course, will come from your own fields, Miss Croft. It would be a fitting symbol of the--a--the bond between the land, the people, and the church. A trinity of mutual support."

"You may have whatever you require from my fields, Mr. Ainsworth, you know that," she said.

"Excellent! I knew we could rely upon your generosity," he beamed. "And Mr. Reed! As a man of science, you will appreciate the--a--the botanical diversity we hope to display. We may even call upon your expertise to identify some of the more unusual specimens the cottagers bring in."

"I should be happy to be of service," said Mr. Reed, though his tone lacked the curate's effusive warmth. He had fallen a step behind, allowing Mr. Ainsworth to walk between himself and Eleanor, and the easy intimacy of their former conversation was quite broken.

They walked on in this new arrangement, the curate discoursing at length upon the proper arrangement of autumn fruits and the theological significance of a bountiful harvest. Eleanor answered him with polite monosyllables, while her thoughts seemed to have retreated to some inner citadel of care. The path grew narrower still, forcing them into single file, with Mr. Ainsworth leading the way, still talking back over his shoulder.

"The light," he was saying, "is of paramount importance. We must not have the marrows obscuring the lower panels of the window, for the depiction of the Good Samaritan is most instructive, and the colours are particularly fine when the afternoon sun strikes them. It is a lesson in--a--in charity which resonates deeply within our community, thanks in no small part, Miss Croft, to your own example."

He stepped aside at a broader part of the path to let her pass, and as she did, Mr. Reed moved forward to her other side, restoring their former proximity.

"Is the list of your burdens now to include the proper placement of gourds?" he murmured, for her ear alone.

A genuine, light-hearted laugh escaped her, the first he had heard that evening. "You are very wicked, Mr. Reed," she whispered back. "Mr. Ainsworth means so well."

"I have no doubt of it," he returned in the same low voice. "Good intentions, I find, are like weeds; they grow in great profusion, but they do not always produce a useful crop."

Their whispered conference was cut short as the path began its gentle descent toward the first scattered cottages of the village. The lights from windows threw warm, yellow oblongs onto the lane, and the smell of woodsmoke hung in the still air. Mr. Ainsworth, his discourse on the festival having run its course, bade them a good evening at the turning to the vicarage, with a final, cheerful reminder about the sheaves of corn.

They were alone again. The silence that fell between them now was different from before; less a comfortable quiet and more a space filled with things unsaid. The spell of the dark cliff-top had been broken by the village and the curate.

"You see," Eleanor said, as they approached the gate of her own house, a respectable stone building set back from the lane with a dark garden in front, "my life is not so very dramatic. It is a matter of nets and sheaves and leaky roofs."

"I do not think that is all it is," he answered. They had stopped at her gate, and he made no move to open it for her. The light from a lamp in her hall spilled out, illuminating his serious, thoughtful face. "There is a difference between a task and a burden, Miss Croft. A task is taken up; a burden is borne. You speak as one who bears a burden you did not choose."

Her eyes fell from his. She looked at the sturdy stone of her house, at the dark, un-flowering garden, at the gate latch under her hand. Everything seemed solid, and fixed, and demanding.

"Perhaps," she said, so softly he had to lean a little to hear. "But what is one to do? One cannot simply set it down. It is not a jug of cider."

"No," he agreed. "It is not. But even the heaviest load is made lighter if one has a companion to walk beside. Not to carry it, perhaps, but only to mark the way and point out the firmer ground."

He did not say more, but the offer, quiet and unassuming as it was, hung in the air between them. It was not a compliment, nor a piece of gallantry, but something far more rare: a simple offer of fellowship. Eleanor felt a warmth spread through her chest that had nothing to do with the lamp in the hall; a feeling so unfamiliar that for a moment it was more frightening than comforting.

She raised her eyes to his again. "The ground here is very stony, Mr. Reed," she said, a faint, tremulous smile touching her lips. "And the path is not always clear."

"I am a naturalist," he replied, with a corresponding smile that transformed his serious features. "I am accustomed to rough terrain."

He opened the gate for her then, and with a quiet "Good-night," she passed through it and walked up the path to her door. He did not leave, but stood watching until the door had closed behind her, and the light in the hall was shut away. For some time after, he remained by the gate, looking at the house as if it were some strange and fascinating specimen, one whose true nature was only beginning to reveal itself. The sea still murmured at the foot of the cliffs, but another, more complex music seemed to have taken its place in the quiet of the village lane.

Fleda's gaze, which had been fixed upon the drawing as if it were a strange and wondrous map to her own soul, at last lifted to meet Mr. Olmney's. The warmth she had felt before did not abate; it deepened, settling into a quiet certainty that was as calming as it was novel. He had not retracted his gaze; he held hers steadily, his own eyes conveying a mixture of earnestness and a gentle, almost reverent curiosity. The world of polite society, with its carefully constructed compliments and veiled intentions, seemed a distant and flimsy thing compared to the solid truth of this moment.

"I think," said Fleda, her voice returning to its normal register, though still imbued with a new softness, "I think perhaps your eye requires no training at all, Mr. Olmney. It may be that you see things too clearly for a world that prefers its pictures varnished."

Before he could answer, the kitchen door opened with a decided, unceremonious push, and Barby entered, her form silhouetted for a moment against the deep purple of the twilight. She carried a large wooden tub, which she set down on the floor with a thud that seemed to punctuate the end of their private conference.

"The doctor and Mr. Douglass have gone up to the house," she announced, not looking at either of them in particular, but addressing the room at large. "Earl says the big kettle is cool enough to be strained now, and he ain't goin' to have it sit all night for the mice to get ideas. He says you know what to do with it, Miss Fleda."

The spell was broken, or rather, it was transformed. The quiet intimacy of the last few moments was swept away by the tide of practical necessity. Fleda felt a brief, sharp pang of regret, as if a beautiful piece of music had been cut short; but then, looking at the tub, and the waiting kettle, and the memory of the drawing fresh in her mind, she felt a different feeling arise. This was the work. This was the charge. And the work was not an interruption of life, but its very substance.

"Thank you, Barby," she said, her voice clear and steady. She closed the sketchbook gently and handed it back to Mr. Olmney. "You will not mind if I put your interesting woman to the test?"

A smile played on his lips. "I shall be fascinated to observe her," he replied, and there was a warmth in his tone that told her he understood perfectly. He did not offer to help, and Fleda was obscurely grateful for it; his help would have turned her once more into a lady being assisted, rather than a farmer at her labour. Instead, he stood back, leaning against the great dresser, sketchbook in hand, an observer who was no longer a stranger.

Fleda took a deep breath of the steam-scented air. "Barby, we need the straining cloth, the fine wool one, I think; and we'll need to set this tub on blocks to get the cask under it tomorrow. Philetus could see to that."

Barby gave a single, sharp nod, a sign of grudging approval that was worth more to Fleda than a volume of compliments. She disappeared into the pantry and returned with a large, clean square of dark woollen cloth. Together, she and Fleda draped it over the mouth of the tub, securing its edges. The task required them to work in close proximity, a silent, efficient partnership. Fleda was acutely aware of Mr. Olmney's presence, of his quiet, attentive gaze, but it no longer made her self-conscious. It was as if his drawing had given her permission to be herself, to be seen in the midst of toil without the need for apology or adornment. She felt the rough texture of the wooden tub, the heat still radiating from the iron kettle, the satisfying pull of her own muscles as she worked, and it all felt right.

With Barby on one side and Fleda on the other, they carefully tipped the great kettle, pouring the warm, dark syrup in a steady stream through the cloth. The liquid was the colour of amber and honey, and the steam that rose from it was thick with the concentrated sweetness of a thousand maple trees. It was a riches, F-l-e-d-a thought, a wealth drawn not from a bank or an inheritance, but from the earth and the sun and their own hard labour. As the last of the syrup gurgled into the tub, she straightened up, brushing a stray lock of hair from her forehead with the back of her hand, and in doing so, unknowingly smeared a bit of soot across her temple.

She caught Mr. Olmney's eye, and he was smiling, a genuine, unguarded smile that crinkled the corners of his eyes. He did not point out the smudge; he simply looked at her, and in his look was all the admiration he had expressed before, redoubled. Fleda felt a blush rise to her cheeks, but it was not a blush of embarrassment. It was the heat of a furnace well-stoked, a fire well-tended.

That evening, the parlour felt strangely confining after the open air and the purposeful clutter of the sugaring camp. Mrs. Rossitur was reclining on the sofa, a book lying unread in her lap, her expression one of gentle, habitual anxiety. The doctor, having partaken of a substantial supper, was now holding forth from a comfortable armchair, his pronouncements on topics ranging from Roman history to the proper digestion of buckwheat cakes filling the air with a sonorous hum. Hugh sat by the fire, whittling a piece of wood with intense concentration, his silence a stark contrast to the doctor's verbosity.

"My dear Fleda," Mrs. Rossitur began, as Fleda entered and took a seat on a low stool near the hearth, "you look quite exhausted. I do wish you would not over-exert yourself so. This farming is a noble idea in theory, but the practical application of it seems to me to be excessively fatiguing."

"I am well, Aunt," Fleda said, her voice calm. "It is a good kind of tired. The kind that comes from doing, not from worrying."

Dr. Quackenboss cleared his throat. "A very astute distinction, Miss Ringgan! Activity, especially that which promotes the circulation of the blood in the open air, is a great panacea. Though I must confess, the particular alchemy of sugar-making is a science of its own. It requires a delicate balance, ahem, of caloric energy and chemical transformation. Mr. Douglass is an empiricist of the first order, a true natural philosopher in his own right, though his nomenclature might be--a--lacking in classical precision."

Mr. Olmney, who had been quietly looking through a portfolio of prints at a side table, now turned to join the conversation. "I found it a most instructive process," he said, his gaze drifting towards Fleda for a brief instant. "There is a kind of elemental honesty to it. One works with the weather, with the trees, with the fire itself. There are no intermediaries."

"Honesty does not pay the bills, Mr. Olmney," Hugh said suddenly, without looking up from his whittling. His tone was sharp. "Nor does it mend a broken fence or bargain for seed. It is all very picturesque for a visitor, but Fleda has to make this place run."

There was an uncomfortable silence. Mrs. Rossitur looked distressed, as if a breach of decorum had occurred which she was powerless to mend. The doctor looked for a moment as if he might offer a lecture on the economics of the agrarian life, but seemed to think better of it.

It was Fleda who answered, her voice even and untroubled. "Hugh is right," she said, to everyone's surprise. "It is not a picture. It is a business, and a difficult one. But honesty is a part of it. Earl's honesty about the sap run, Barby's honesty in her work, the honesty of a tree that gives what it can when the conditions are right. That is the currency we deal in here, Hugh. And I believe it is a sound one." She looked at her cousin, not with defiance, but with a quiet appeal for understanding. "I am not playing at being a farmer. I am learning to be one. And I will need your help, not your doubts."

Hugh's hands stilled. He looked at his sister, truly looked at her, and the hard line of his mouth softened. He gave a curt nod and resumed his whittling, but the sharp, angry scrapes of the knife were replaced by a slower, more thoughtful rhythm.

Mr. Olmney had watched the exchange with keen interest. He now addressed Fleda directly, his tone one of respectful inquiry. "Mrs. Rossitur mentioned that you have taken over the farm accounts, Miss Ringgan. That must be a considerable undertaking in itself."

"It is a world of figures that do not always add up as they should," Fleda admitted. "My uncle was a good man, but not, perhaps, the most meticulous of book-keepers. There are ledgers to be reconciled and letters from suppliers that I am only just beginning to comprehend."

"Ah, the mercantile aspect!" exclaimed the doctor. "A necessary evil! It is where the pure philosophy of agriculture meets the sordid reality of commerce. I myself have had some small experience in the matter, having once written a paper on the economic fallacies of the South Sea Bubble--"

"I was thinking," Mr. Olmney interjected smoothly, cutting off a lecture Fleda knew from experience could last an hour, "that the principles of rational accounting are universal. My own father was a merchant, and I spent a rather dull year in his counting-house before escaping to the university. The work was tedious, but the logic of it was compelling. If you would ever permit me to look over any particularly knotty problems, I should be honoured to offer whatever small assistance I might."

He made the offer so quietly, so deferentially, that it could not possibly be construed as an intrusion or a slight upon her own capabilities. He was not offering to take the burden from her, but merely to provide a tool, like offering a better lamp to one who is reading in the dark.

"That is very kind of you, Mr. Olmney," Fleda said, a genuine gratitude warming her. "I may indeed take you up on your offer. Some of Mr. Skillcorn's invoices, in particular, seem to defy all known laws of arithmetic."

Mrs. Rossitur gave a little sigh of relief, sensing the tension had passed. "Well, that is very good of you, Mr. Olmney. Fleda does need a sensible head to help her. It is all too much for a young lady."

"On the contrary, madam," Mr. Olmney said, with a slight bow in Mrs. Rossitur's direction but with his eyes on Fleda. "I believe Miss Ringgan's head is the most sensible one in the room. But even the most capable general can benefit from a good map."

The next morning, Fleda rose before the sun, a new energy coursing through her. The conversation of the previous night had settled something within her. The path ahead was still steep and uncertain, but she no longer felt she was walking it entirely alone. After a quick breakfast, she went not to the parlour, but to her uncle's small, dusty office, a room she had until now found oppressive and confusing.

The desk was piled high with papers: old receipts, catalogues for farm implements, letters from neighbours, and the thick, leather-bound ledgers. Before, this chaos had represented only a burden, a tangle of responsibilities she feared she could never unravel. Now, she saw it differently. It was a puzzle, a story waiting to be deciphered.

She pulled out the main ledger and opened it. Her uncle's handwriting was sprawling and inconsistent. Entries were crowded together, with notes scrawled in the margins. It was daunting. She remembered Mr. Olmney's offer and was tempted, for a moment, to wait for his assistance. But then she looked at her own hands, still slightly sticky with syrup from the night before, and thought of the drawing. He had not drawn a woman waiting to be rescued.

She would do what she could herself, first. She would put her own house in order.

She took a clean sheet of paper and began, methodically, to work her way through the most recent entries, creating a new, clear summary of expenses and income. The work was slow and painstaking. She had to cross-reference entries with loose receipts, decipher cryptic notes--"Sold J.P. sow, less 2 bu. corn"--and make educated guesses about dates and quantities. The sun was high in the sky when a light knock came at the door.

It was Mr. Olmney. He held a small, neatly-bound book in his hand. "Forgive my intrusion," he said. "I was on my way out for a walk and saw your light. I thought you might find this useful." He held out the book. Its title was "The Farmer's Accountant, or, The Principles of Double-Entry Book-Keeping as Applied to the Rural Economy."

Fleda took the book, its crisp pages and clear type a stark contrast to the chaotic ledger on her desk. "Mr. Olmney, this is... where did you find this?"

"It was in my trunk," he said with a small smile. "A relic of my time in the counting-house. I confess I brought it with me on the off-chance that I might find the intellectual life of the country stultifying and need some complex problems to occupy my mind. It seems you have more compelling problems than I could have invented."

She laughed, a genuine, easy laugh. "You came prepared for boredom, and instead you found a farm in disarray."

"I found a farm in transition," he corrected gently. "Which is far more interesting." He glanced at the papers on her desk, at the neat column of figures she had started. "I see you have already made a formidable start."

"I am attempting to bring order to chaos," she said. "Or at least to understand the nature of the chaos I have inherited."

"May I?" he asked, indicating a chair. At her nod, he sat down, not taking the ledger from her, but simply looking on as she explained what she had discovered. He listened intently, asking a pertinent question here and there, pointing to a passage in the little book he had brought that clarified a principle of debit and credit, suggesting a way to categorize expenses that would make them easier to track in the future. He was not a teacher lecturing a student, but a fellow scholar collaborating on a difficult text. In his presence, the daunting task became a fascinating intellectual challenge. The figures on the page were no longer just numbers; they were the story of the farm, the ebb and flow of its lifeblood, and Fleda felt a rising sense of mastery as, together, they began to make it legible. The burden of care was still hers, and hers alone, but she was learning, with his quiet encouragement, to read its language. And in that, she was finding a satisfaction as deep and pure as the sweetness of the maple syrup she had strained with her own hands.
